V04-A-001: Forgiveness is often confused with excusing, but the two are closer to opposites than to near relations. To excuse someone is to decide that what they did was not really their fault: they were tired, misled or under pressure, and so there is nothing to hold against them. This is why forgiveness can be offered only by someone who has been wronged, and why it can cost her something: the resentment she surrenders was hers by right. An excuse costs nothing of the kind, since it removes the very ground of complaint. It follows that the more readily we excuse, the less there is left for us to forgive. A person who explains away every injury may seem generous, but he has quietly declined to treat others as responsible for what they do. To forgive, by contrast, is to accept that the wrong was real and was theirs, and then to give up the resentment one is entitled to feel.
V04-A-002: People who plan a project routinely underestimate how long it will take, even when they have finished similar projects late many times before. What makes the error puzzling is not its existence but its persistence, since experience ought to correct it. The usual explanation is that planners take an inside view: they picture the particular steps of the task in front of them and add up the time each step seems to need. Such a picture is built out of intentions, and intentions contain no interruptions. The proposed remedy is to take an outside view, setting aside the details of the project and asking how long projects of the same general kind have actually taken. This feels like throwing information away, because it ignores everything the planner knows about her own case. In fact it restores the information that matters most, the record of how such projects usually go wrong, which the inside view had quietly left out. Real projects, by contrast, are seldom spared them: an illness, a late delivery or a resignation befalls almost every one, though no single one could have been foreseen.
V04-A-003: When a city renames a street, the new name appears overnight on signs and maps, but it often takes a generation to appear in everyday speech. That knowledge is spread across thousands of small habits: residents give directions by the old name, shopkeepers print it on their cards, and older people use it to locate their memories. An official order can change the label, but it cannot reach what people already know, and so the old name lingers in conversation long after it has vanished from the signs. Newcomers, who never knew the old name, adopt the new one almost at once. For a while the city speaks in two vocabularies, and the change is complete only when those who learned the old name are no longer there to use it. The reason is that a street name is not only an official label but also a piece of shared local knowledge.
V04-A-004: Long before electricity carried messages, France in the 1790s began building chains of hilltop towers whose movable arms could be set in many distinct positions, each standing for a letter, word or phrase. An operator watched the neighbouring tower through a telescope, copied its signal and passed it on, so that a message could cross the country far faster than any rider. The system was impressive, but its limits were as instructive as its speed. It worked only in daylight and in clear weather, and every tower needed trained staff who did nothing but watch and repeat. Above all, it was built to serve the state, which saw in rapid communication a means of holding a large territory together. Private citizens were generally not permitted to send messages on it, and the network was never meant to become a public service. The speed of a message, in other words, mattered less to the history of communication than the question of who was permitted to send one.
V04-A-005: Economists have long puzzled over why many prices change so rarely, even when the costs behind them move every week. One explanation points to the costs of changing a price itself. Each such cost is small, but if a firm expects the change in its own costs to be temporary, even a small expense can make waiting the sensible choice. The puzzle does not disappear entirely, however, because the sums involved often look far too small to explain the delays observed. A second explanation therefore looks to customers rather than to firms: people may resent frequent price changes and take their business elsewhere. On this account, a stable price is part of what a firm sells. A restaurant that raises the price of a single dish must reprint its menus, and a shop must relabel its shelves and explain the change to regular customers.
V04-A-006: A lichen looks like a single plant, a crust or a leafy fringe on a rock or a branch, but it is in fact a partnership. A fungus provides the structure and holds water, while an alga or a bacterium living inside it makes food from sunlight. Together they can live where neither could survive alone: on bare stone, on desert soil, on the bark of trees in the coldest forests. Because a lichen has no roots and no protective outer skin, it takes in water and nutrients directly from rain and from the air around it. Many species disappear from city centres where sulphur dioxide is common, and some return when the air is cleaned. For this reason, surveys of lichens have long been used as a cheap way of reading the quality of the air in a district. A lichen does not so much measure pollution as record its history, since it grows slowly and responds to years of exposure rather than to a single bad day. Yet the very openness that lets it live on bare rock leaves it with no defence against whatever else the air contains.
V04-A-007: Two drivers take the same corner too fast on the same wet evening, and both are equally careless. One reaches home without incident; a child steps into the road in front of the other. We blame the second driver far more severely, and so, in all likelihood, does he. One response is to call our reaction an error: the two are equally guilty, and the second is merely unluckier. This keeps the principle of control intact, but at a cost, for it asks us to treat the grief and remorse of the second driver as a kind of confusion. Another response accepts that luck shapes what we are answerable for, and concludes that the principle was never as firm as it seemed. Neither response is comfortable, and the discomfort is itself the discovery: our practice of blame rests on two commitments that do not fit together. Yet if blame should track only what lies within a person's control, this difference is hard to justify, since the child's step was no doing of his.
V04-A-008: Experts are often poor at explaining their subject to beginners, and the usual explanation, that they are impatient or careless, misses the deeper difficulty. Once we know something, it becomes very hard to imagine not knowing it. The expert reads a diagram and sees at once what matters; she cannot easily recover the experience of looking at the same lines and seeing nothing in particular. Steps that once cost her effort have become invisible, and so she leaves them out, not from haste but because they no longer seem like steps. The beginner, meanwhile, is unable to say what is missing, since knowing what one does not understand already requires some understanding. The gap therefore persists without either party seeing it clearly. The most reliable remedy is to watch beginners attempt the task, since their errors reveal what neither they nor the expert could have put into words.
V04-A-009: Historians of the last few centuries have relied heavily on private letters. A letter was written for one reader, often in haste, and it preserved opinions and feelings that its writer would never have put into print. Families kept such letters in drawers and attics, and a great many of them eventually found their way into libraries and archives. Messages of this kind are easy to delete, and the accounts that hold them are often closed when their owners die. No one clears out an attic full of messages after a funeral, because there is no attic to clear. Future historians may therefore find that the age which wrote more than any before it has left fewer intimate records behind. Today, much of that private correspondence has moved to email and messaging services, where it is stored on servers that its writers do not control.
V04-A-010: The practice of holding ships and travellers in isolation for a fixed period before they could enter a port took shape in Mediterranean trading cities in the late Middle Ages, in response to repeated outbreaks of plague. Those who devised it had no idea that the disease was carried by microbes; many of them believed it spread through corrupted air. A waiting period long enough for the sick to show their illness could catch infections whatever their mechanism. The episode is sometimes told as a story of luck, as if officials stumbled on a sound practice for the wrong reasons. That reading undervalues what they did, which was to act on a pattern they could observe instead of waiting for a theory they did not have. Public health has often had to work this way, and it still does whenever a new illness spreads faster than its explanation. Yet the rule could still do some good, because it did not depend on knowing the cause, only on noticing that sickness tended to arrive with people and goods from places already afflicted.
V04-A-011: Standard reasoning suggests that a firm should pay no more than it must, offering the lowest wage at which it can fill its posts. One reason is that a worker who earns more than she could get elsewhere has more to lose if she is dismissed, and so she has reason to work carefully even when no one is watching. A better wage also draws more applicants, letting the firm choose among them, and it reduces the cost of training replacements for those who leave. On this view, a higher wage can pay for itself, since what the firm spends on pay it partly recovers in effort, in selection and in lower turnover. The argument has a limit, however: it works best where effort is hard to monitor and departures are costly, and where output is easily measured, the lowest wage may still be the sensible choice. Yet many employers knowingly pay above that level, and they are not simply being generous.
V04-A-012: A river delta is built from mud and sand that the river carries down from its basin and drops where it meets the sea. As long as this supply continues, the delta can keep pace with the slow sinking of its own soft ground and with the waves that wear its edges away. Large dams interrupt the process at its source. Their reservoirs trap much of the sediment that once travelled downstream, and the water released below them is comparatively clear. Deprived of fresh material, many deltas have begun to shrink, even where the sea itself has risen only a little. Coastal engineers can build walls against the waves, but no wall can replace the sediment that the river no longer brings. The protection of a delta, then, may depend less on such walls than on what happens hundreds of kilometres upstream.
V04-A-013: We often criticise people for what they believe: for trusting a rumour, for clinging to a prejudice, for refusing to accept plain evidence. Such criticism seems to assume that belief is under our control, as an action is. Yet it plainly is not, at least not directly: no one can decide by an effort of will to believe that it is raining while looking at a clear sky. We control what we attend to, which sources we consult, and how long we keep looking before we settle a question. A person who believes a rumour has usually done something earlier: declined to check, preferred a pleasing source, stopped asking once the answer suited him. Criticism of belief is best understood as criticism of these habits of inquiry, which are within our reach even when the belief itself is not. This explains why we excuse a person who was deceived by forged evidence that no reasonable inquiry could have exposed. It does not follow that the criticism is confused, for we can be answerable for things we cannot choose at a stroke.
V04-A-014: People tend to value things more highly when they have helped to make them, even when the result is clumsy. A shelf assembled from a flat pack, a cake baked from a mix, a vegetable bed dug by hand: each seems worth more to its maker than an identical one bought ready-made. What seems to matter is completion, the sense of having turned raw materials into something that works. This suggests that the extra value is a kind of reward for competence, since the finished object becomes evidence of what its maker can do. Sellers have learned to use the tendency by leaving a small, satisfying step for the customer to complete. The step must be easy enough to succeed at, however, since a task that ends in failure produces frustration rather than pride. Yet effort alone seems not to be the cause, for a task that is abandoned halfway rarely leaves its maker with the same attachment.
V04-A-015: Styles of dress seem to return at fairly regular intervals: wide trousers, bold patterns and certain colours disappear for a couple of decades and then come back as if they were new. Part of the answer lies with the young, for whom a style their parents wore looks dated while a style their grandparents wore can look charmingly unfamiliar. Each generation of young buyers therefore rejects what it grew up seeing and reaches back past it to something its members never saw worn in earnest. Designers and shops, who need a reason to sell new clothes every season, are happy to encourage the revival. The returning style is rarely an exact copy, however; it comes back altered to suit new fabrics, new bodies and new ideas of comfort. Why should fashions move in such cycles rather than wandering at random?
V04-A-016: Until the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own time, set by the position of the sun, so that noon in one town fell a few minutes earlier or later than noon in the next. For travellers on foot or on horseback the differences hardly mattered, since no one moved fast enough to notice them. Railways changed this. A timetable that listed departures in a dozen local times was a recipe for missed connections and, on single tracks, for collisions. Railway companies therefore began to run their trains on a single standard time, and the towns along their lines gradually adjusted their clocks to match. Some resisted for a while, fitting the town clock with two minute hands, one for local time and one for the railway's. In the end, it was the timetable, not the sun, that told most people what time it was.
V04-A-017: Software that anyone may copy, change and share for free poses an obvious puzzle for economics. Thousands of skilled programmers contribute to such projects without being paid by them, and the results compete with products built by firms that charge for theirs. Part of the answer is that many contributors are in fact paid, by employers who depend on the software and find it cheaper to improve a shared tool than to build a private one. For her, the rewards are of a different kind: the pleasure of solving a problem, the respect of peers who can see exactly what she did, and a public record of skill that later employers may value. The last of these rewards is the most economic, and it depends on openness itself, since a contribution hidden inside a firm's private code would be visible to no one outside it. The puzzle is partly dissolved, then, by noticing that open work produces a currency of reputation that closed work cannot. But this explains only the contributions that some company wants; it does not explain the volunteer who spends her evenings fixing an obscure fault.
V04-A-018: The roots of most land plants are joined to fungi that extend far into the soil, trading water and minerals for sugars that the plant makes in its leaves. Because a single fungus can connect to several plants at once, some writers have described forests as communities in which trees share food and warnings through an underground network. What remains uncertain is how much moves, how often, and whether the movement benefits the receiving plant rather than the fungus that carries it. A fungus is not a public utility; it is an organism with interests of its own, and it may move sugar wherever it gains most from doing so. Describing it as a channel for cooperation between trees may therefore attribute to the trees a purpose that belongs, if to anyone, to the fungus. None of this makes the network less remarkable; it makes the question of who is helping whom more interesting than the popular story allows. The picture is appealing, and it is not simply invented: substances have been traced moving from one plant to another through fungal threads.
V04-A-019: It is often said that there is no arguing about taste. In such conversations, people rarely try to prove that a work is good; instead they point to features of it that the other person may have missed. Look at how the ending answers the opening, one says, or listen to what the bass is doing under the melody. The aim is not to win agreement by force of logic but to change what the other person perceives. When it works, the listener does not feel defeated; she feels that she now hears something she did not hear before. Disputes about taste are therefore real disputes, even if they are settled by attention rather than by proof. If that were true, however, the long conversations people have about films, novels and music would be pointless, and they plainly are not.
V04-A-020: The placebo effect is often mentioned with a shrug, as if to say that a patient who improves after a sugar pill was never really ill, or only imagined getting better. Studies that separate different kinds of outcome suggest that the shrug is wrong in one way and right in another. On objective measures, such as the size of a tumour or the level of an infection, dummy treatments tend to achieve little. On symptoms that pass through experience, above all pain, nausea and fatigue, they can produce changes that patients report as genuine relief. It would be equally mistaken, however, to treat a dummy pill as a remedy like any other, since relief that rests on expectation may fade once the expectation is withdrawn. Those who shrug at the effect are therefore right about the tumour and wrong about the pain, and their error is to treat a change in how illness feels as no change at all.
V04-A-021: Audiences at concerts of classical music are expected to stay silent between the movements of a symphony and to applaud only at the very end. Newcomers who clap after the first movement are met with frowns, and they may feel they have exposed their ignorance. Yet the rule is younger than it looks. The silence now demanded grew up later, alongside a view of the symphony as a single unbroken argument that applause would interrupt. There is something to be said for that view, since a pause between movements can itself be part of the music's effect. But a convention that makes first-time listeners feel unwelcome has a cost too, especially as many of the works were written for noisier halls. In earlier centuries, audiences often applauded between movements, and sometimes in the middle of one when a passage pleased them.
V04-A-022: For much of history, most people in many parts of Europe had a single given name, and a village rarely needed more to tell its members apart. As populations grew and rulers began to tax and count their subjects more carefully, a single name was no longer enough. Many of these additions are still easy to read: a family called Smith or Baker descends, at some remove, from a person known by his work. At first such names could change from one generation to the next, since a baker's son might become a carter. Only gradually did they become fixed and hereditary, passed down whatever the bearer actually did for a living. The surname, in other words, began as a description and ended as a label. Clerks and neighbours added a second name to distinguish one John from another, drawn from a trade, a place, a father or some personal feature.
V04-A-023: Insurance exists to spread the cost of misfortune, but it can also change the behaviour of the people it protects. Economists call changes of this kind moral hazard, though the term implies more wickedness than the problem involves: neither the driver nor the firm has decided to cheat anyone. Insurers respond in ways that are familiar to anyone who has read a policy. They require the insured to bear the first part of any loss, offer lower premiums to those who install alarms, and refuse to pay where carelessness was gross. Each of these devices leaves the insured with some of the risk, which is precisely the point. Full protection would remove the very incentive that keeps losses rare, so a policy that covered everything would soon cost more than anyone would pay. A driver whose car is fully insured has a little less reason to park it carefully, and a firm insured against fire has a little less reason to spend money on sprinklers.
V04-A-024: Why is the sky dark at night? The question sounds childish, but it troubled astronomers for centuries, because a simple argument seemed to show that the night sky should blaze. If the universe were infinite, unchanging and evenly filled with stars, then every line of sight, extended far enough, would end on the surface of some star. Distant stars appear fainter, but there would be more of them in proportion, and the two effects would cancel exactly. The whole sky would then shine about as brightly as the surface of a typical star. The darkness we see therefore tells us that at least one of the assumptions is false. The modern answer rejects the assumption that the universe is unchanging: it has a finite age, so light from stars beyond a certain distance has not yet had time to reach us. The expansion of space adds a further effect, stretching the light of distant sources until much of it falls outside the range our eyes can see.
V04-A-025: A label beside an object in a museum seems a modest thing: a name, a date, a sentence or two of context. Yet it shapes looking more than most visitors realise, telling them what kind of attention to pay: whether to admire a technique, to place an object in history or to feel the weight of an event. None of this is sinister, since without labels most objects would remain mute to all but specialists. The difficulty lies in the order of events. Many visitors read the label first and then glance at the object to confirm what they have been told, so that they can leave having learned the label's lesson while hardly seeing what it described. Some curators have answered this by placing the text a few steps away, so that the eye meets the object before it meets the words.
